    <title>The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery</title>
    <updated>2026-10-13T11:28:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.18933v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.18933v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Modern coding agents are fundamentally reshaping the role of human input for computational research: they write code, launch in silico experiments, analyze their results, and autonomously operate with ever-increasing time horizons. Despite these developments, fully autonomous research agents suffer from a limited ideation radius and myopic hill-climbing search dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce The Agentic Scientist, an end-to-end distributed pipeline for human researchers to conduct computational research alongside modern coding agents. Building on its predecessor, our system decomposes research into task drafting, idea generation, planning, sandboxed experimentation, result aggregation, baseline and ablation construction, post-hoc analysis, and report writing. Importantly, each step in the pipeline is powered by the next generation of coding agents and leverages agentic self-verification. The overall research process is driven by a meta-controller that manages parallel research agents and enforces rubric verification at each stage. This design enables the same orchestration layer to be reused across heterogeneous domains with different execution environments, agentic coding harnesses, and evaluation metrics. Our system can be used across a spectrum of autonomy: either as a co-scientist tool or to perform end-to-end scientific investigation. Within the co-scientist setting, we leveraged a development version of our system to submit a single research paper, which got accepted for publication at ALIFE 2026. We further apply The Agentic Scientist fully autonomously to open problem-solving tasks in machine learning, and demonstrate the system's capability of scientific discovery across different domains of computational research. Our ablations suggest that reliable scientific autonomy depends not only on base model capabilities, but also on the cross-agent orchestration layer.</summary>

bounded_raw_excerpts.rubric_protocol_drift_section_html:
Rubric-specification sensitivity.

We observe a failure mode introduced by structural limitations of rubric-based verification: rubrics check only the criteria they enumerate, so they cannot catch violations of constraints that were never stated, and human researchers remain responsible for specifying tasks precisely and verifying that results respect their full intent. In two of the three Pi runs, we observed that the agent also modified the test-time evaluation procedure itself (e.g., using kk-sample majority voting instead of the baseline’s pass@1), which inflates the reported validation accuracy without improving the training algorithm. The task prompt asks the agent to improve the “training” algorithm, but never explicitly requires a fixed evaluation procedure. No initial rubric item covers this evaluation-protocol integrity. Neither the evaluator nor the rubric gates flagged these programs, and we identified them after a manual post-hoc audit. After excluding protocol-violating programs, Pi still reaches high scores faster and more consistently than all other agents.
bounded_raw_excerpts.manuscript_limits_section_html:
Limitations.

At present, The Agentic Scientist could be enhanced by a reliable literature-to-code pipeline for constructing state-of-the-art baselines. The task drafting pipeline (Section 3.1) is also not fully robust: it can draft simple tasks such as circle packing from a research brief, but for larger tasks such as the world-model and tabular distribution-shift tasks in Section 5, it may fail to produce an initial program, evaluators, and task contract that exactly match the full Agentic Scientist scaffold. Reliable task drafting nevertheless remains an important capability, since it removes the last manual step between a research brief and an automated campaign. Unlike AI Scientist-v1 and AI Scientist-v2 (Lu et al., 2024b; Yamada et al., 2025), The Agentic Scientist only explicitly searches the literature during manuscript writing rather than during initial ideation. That being said, we repeatedly observe that coding agents leverage general web access to inform idea investigation. Beyond these capability gaps, the system’s verification is only as complete as its task-specific evaluators and rubrics, which may omit methodological errors or reward unintended shortcuts. Results that pass verification should therefore still be inspected and validated by human researchers. Although the cross-harness and model evaluation covers 70 campaigns, its paper-level metric is an AI-reviewer proxy rather than full evidence of scientific correctness, and only the Error Diffusion paper underwent external peer review. Our evaluations are also restricted to computational machine learning, so they do not establish the feasibility of transferring the orchestration workflow to domains requiring physical experiments or human-subject studies. Finally, for autoillustrate we present additional component-specific limitations and failure cases in Section E.3.
